evidence: USGS VHP: injected ash is mostly removed from the stratosphere within several days to weeks; SO2 converts to sulfuric acid aerosols that reflect sunlight; several eruptions in the past century cooled the surface for periods of one to three years.

National Geographic: scientists describe Earth in terms of spheres (lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere); since life exists on the ground, in the air and in the water, the biosphere overlaps all these spheres.
National Geographic: a hydrosphere is the total amount of water on a planet, on the surface, underground and in the air; it can be liquid, vapor or ice.
USGS Water Science School: a large oak tree can transpire 40,000 gallons (151,000 liters) per year; transpiration releases water vapor through leaf stomata.
Britannica, Mineral: "Ice, the solid state of water (H2O), is considered a mineral, but liquid water is not."
Britannica: a mineral is a naturally occurring homogeneous solid with a definite chemical composition and a highly ordered atomic arrangement; it is usually formed by inorganic processes.
IMA-CNMNC (Elements 2024): the number of recognized mineral species is just above 6000; the CNMNC approves new species regularly, with over a hundred accepted each year in recent times.
Britannica, Quartz: silica, or silicon dioxide (SiO2); varieties include amethyst (purple), citrine (yellow), rose quartz (pink) and smoky quartz.

USGS FAQ: a rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals; common rocks include granite, basalt, limestone and sandstone; common minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica, amphibole, olivine and calcite.
Geology.com: hematite colors range red to brown and black to gray to silver, yet it always produces a reddish streak; the name is from the Greek haimatitis, blood-red.
Geology.com: specimens with metallic luster have the brightness of a metal and are always opaque (galena pictured); quartz usually has a vitreous luster.
Britannica, Mohs hardness: ~2.2 fingernail, ~3.2 copper penny, ~5.1 pocketknife, ~5.5 glass plate.
Britannica: calcite to fluorite is an increase in hardness of approximately 25 percent; corundum to diamond is a hardness increase of more than 300 percent.
Britannica: devised (1812) by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs; ten minerals from talc to diamond in the listed order.
Geology.com: nicknamed Fool's Gold for its gold color and metallic luster; streak greenish black to brownish black. Its streak-test page lists gold's streak as metallic gold yellow.

Geology.com: streak is the color of a mineral's powder, made by scraping it across unglazed porcelain (a streak plate); its hematite page notes the highly variable appearance but consistent reddish streak.
Britannica, Feldspar: "Feldspars make up more than half of Earth's crust."

Britannica, Granite: rich in quartz and feldspar, minor muscovite and biotite; a photomicrograph caption shows pinkish feldspar and nearly white quartz (red to pink feldspar is typical of many granites).
Britannica, Mica: perfect cleavage into thin elastic sheets; biotite is black, brown, red to red-brown, greenish brown and blue-green.
Britannica, Quartz: the second most abundant mineral in Earth's crust after feldspar; Mohs hardness 7; highly resistant to weathering, it concentrates in sandstones and other detrital rocks.
Britannica, Sand: quartz is the commonest mineral because it is abundant in rocks, comparatively hard, has practically no cleavage, is nearly insoluble in water and does not decompose.
Britannica, Silicate mineral: silicon and oxygen are the two most abundant elements in Earth's crust; the silicates make up about 95 percent of Earth's crust and upper mantle.
Britannica: basalt is an extrusive igneous rock, dark and comparatively rich in iron and magnesium. National Geographic, Crust: oceanic crust is mostly composed of different types of basalts.
NPS: cooling causes contraction which causes fracturing; most columns are hexagonal (three to seven sides); Devils Postpile in California is a best-known example.

Britannica: granite is a coarse- or medium-grained intrusive igneous rock, the most common plutonic rock of Earth's crust. National Geographic, Crust: continental crust is mostly composed of different types of granites.

Britannica, Igneous rock: intrusive magma cools slowly and crystallizes completely, with minerals visible to the naked eye; erupted lava is chilled so quickly that minerals have little or no chance to grow, giving microscopic crystals or glass.
Britannica: obsidian is igneous rock occurring as a natural glass formed by the rapid cooling of viscous lava; rising viscosity prevents crystallization.
Britannica: slow cooling at depth permits ion migration and crystal growth; extruded magma is chilled so quickly that the individual minerals have little or no chance to grow.
Britannica, Sedimentary rock: lithification by compaction under the weight of overlying material and cementation, as minerals precipitate in the pore spaces between grains.

Britannica, Limestone: composed mainly of calcium carbonate, usually as calcite or aragonite; in many cases the grains are microscopic fragments of fossil animal shells; lime-secreting organisms are primary agents.
Britannica, Sandstone: sand-sized grains 0.063 to 2 mm in diameter, framework mainly quartz, with a chemical cement of silica or calcium carbonate or a fine matrix.
Canadian Encyclopedia: only about 5% of Earth's crust is sedimentary rock, but it covers 70-75% of the exposed surface. Britannica also gives about 5 percent by volume of the crust.
Britannica, Shale: fine-grained, laminated rock of silt- and clay-sized particles that splits into thin layers; roughly 70 percent of the sedimentary rocks in Earth's crust.
Britannica: the slab came from the Carrara quarries in Tuscany; early in the morning on September 13, 1501, the young artist got to work; he finished in 1504.

USGS FAQ: foliation forms when pressure squeezes flat or elongate minerals so they become aligned; granite gneiss and biotite schist are strongly banded or foliated; limestone is made of minerals that are not flat or elongate.
Britannica: marble is granular limestone or dolomite that has recrystallized under heat, pressure and aqueous solutions; the main mineral in marble is calcite.

USGS FAQ: metamorphism does not melt the rocks but transforms them into denser, more compact rocks; new minerals form by rearrangement or reactions with fluids; parent rocks can be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic.
Britannica, Slate: fine-grained metamorphic rock from mudstone or shale that splits into thin slabs; cleavage is the result of pressure; used for roofing and flooring and blackboards.

Britannica, Corundum: aluminum oxide (Al2O3), 9 on the Mohs scale, the hardest natural substance after diamond; pure corundum is colorless; ruby's red comes from chromium, blue sapphire's from iron and titanium.

Britannica, Gemstone: minerals highly prized for beauty, durability and rarity; durability lets a stone retain its polish and withstand constant handling; pearl, red coral and amber are organic, noncrystalline gem materials.
Britannica, Ore mineral: an ore is a natural aggregation of minerals that can be mined and sold for profit; hematite and magnetite are iron ore minerals, chalcopyrite a copper ore mineral.

Britannica, Ore deposit: all ore deposits are mineral deposits but the reverse is not true; ore deposit is an economic term, mineral deposit geological; profitability depends on concentration, size, mining and transport costs and prices.
Soils 4 Teachers (SSSA): R (bedrock) is a mass of rock such as granite, basalt, quartzite, limestone or sandstone; this is not soil and is located under the C horizon.

Oregon State Extension: a typical soil in good condition is about 45% mineral matter, 25% air, 25% water and 5% organic matter; minerals are tiny rock fragments classed as sand, silt and clay; clay needs a powerful microscope to see.

Oregon State Extension: five soil-forming factors (parent material, climate, living organisms, topography, time); whenever these five are the same the soil will be the same; if one varies the soils differ.

Soils 4 Teachers: O mostly organic matter such as decomposing leaves; A topsoil, minerals with organic matter; E leached, missing in some soils; B subsoil where leached minerals accumulate; C parent material.
Soils 4 Teachers: soils are complex mixtures of minerals, water, air, organic matter and countless organisms that are the decaying remains of once-living things.

Britannica, Quartzite: sandstone converted into solid quartz rock by silica cementation or recrystallization under heat and pressure; breaks through, not around, the sand grains, producing a smooth surface; weathers slowly, forming prominent ridges.
National Geographic, Mantle: in most places, the geothermal gradient is about 25 degrees C per kilometer of depth.

Berkeley Lab (July 2011): KamLAND, a sphere of a thousand metric tons of scintillating mineral oil deep underground in Japan, measured geoneutrinos; radioactive decay supplies only about half the Earth's heat, the rest primordial heat left over from formation and possibly others.

National Geographic, Mantle: convection currents transfer hot, buoyant magma to the lithosphere at plate boundaries and hot spots, and transfer denser, cooler material back into Earth's interior through subduction.

National Geographic, Core: the primary contributors to heat in the core are radioactive decay, leftover heat from planetary formation, and heat released as the liquid outer core solidifies near its boundary with the inner core.
USGS This Dynamic Earth: when two continents meet head-on neither is subducted and the crust buckles upward; the collision of India into Asia 50 million years ago began building the Himalayas.
USGS This Dynamic Earth: divergent boundaries occur where plates move apart and new crust is created by magma pushing up from the mantle.
Thingvellir National Park: at Thingvellir the plates break apart and the land between subsides; away from the plate boundaries the activity is about two centimetres a year.
USGS This Dynamic Earth: the Nazca Plate is subducted under South America, lifting the Andes; oceanic-continental convergence sustains volcanoes such as those in the Andes and the Cascade Range.

USGS This Dynamic Earth: when two oceanic plates converge one is usually subducted, forming a trench; the Marianas Trench, paralleling the Mariana Islands, marks where the Pacific Plate converges against the Philippine Plate; island arcs are generally curved.
USGS This Dynamic Earth: transform boundaries, where crust is neither produced nor destroyed as plates slide horizontally past each other; the San Andreas fault zone in California is one on land.

GFZ press release (06/08/2017): the Hawaiian-Emperor chain's peculiar 60 degrees bend, between the older Emperor part (about 80 to 47 million years old) and the younger Hawaiian part; a new study shows both plate-motion change and plume drift play an important role.
NOAA Ocean Service: each island or submerged seamount in the chain is successively older toward the northwest; the age progression records the Pacific plate's motion.

USGS This Dynamic Earth: in 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson hypothesized the Hawaiian-Emperor chain resulted from the Pacific Plate moving over a deep, stationary hotspot; volcanoes grow over it and are carried away.

NPS: the North American Plate has been moving west-southwest over the hotspot, so a chain of volcanic centers extends across the Snake River Plain to Yellowstone; hot springs and geysers are the current manifestation of the hotspot.
USGS YVO: the hotspot left a trail that begins in northern Nevada and southern Oregon about 17 million years ago, becoming younger across southern Idaho to Yellowstone National Park.
Britannica, Normal fault: the Basin and Range Province is made up of an extensive network of horsts and grabens.
USGS FAQ: a fault is a fracture or zone of fractures between two blocks of rock; faults allow the blocks to move relative to each other.
Britannica: the block of rock above the fault is the hanging wall and the block below is the footwall.
USGS FAQ: normal fault, the block above the fault moves downward relative to the block below; occurs in response to extension.
USGS FAQ: reverse (thrust) fault, the upper block moves up and over the lower block; common in areas of compression.
USGS FAQ: strike-slip fault, the two blocks slide past one another; the San Andreas Fault is an example of a right lateral fault.
Britannica, Reverse fault: thrust faults are reverse faults with a low angle of dip, less than 45 degrees; found predominantly in mountain ranges and where plates converge.
USGS: P waves are the first waves to vibrate a building; S waves are the most damaging, because buildings are more easily damaged from horizontal motion than vertical; surface waves arrive last.
USGS: ShakeAlert is not earthquake prediction; it detects an earthquake that has already started and alerts before shaking arrives.
PNSN: P waves are compressional waves that deform the ground in the direction of travel, faster than other seismic waves, 5 or 6 km/s in rock, and move through solid or liquid.
PNSN: S waves are shear waves that deform the ground perpendicular to their travel, about 3 km/s, and are unable to pass through liquids.
USGS: ShakeAlert works because P-waves travel almost twice as fast as the damaging S-waves and surface waves; the USGS-operated system serves California, Oregon and Washington.
PNSN: surface waves travel more slowly than body waves but can have very large amplitudes; Rayleigh waves produce a long rolling motion; Love waves shake side to side.
USGS: 5:12 AM, April 18, 1906; rupturing the northernmost 296 miles (477 kilometers) of the San Andreas fault.

USGS: a fence near Bolinas offset about 8.5 feet along the fault trace; the S-shaped fence diagram greatly exaggerates the distortion, which is spread over many miles and can only be seen with precise instruments.
problem: The fact (8.5 ft offset) is right, but card 16.c1 says the fence "had been slowly bent out of line before it broke" and "torn apart". USGS says the pre-quake bending is spread over many miles and is invisible without precise instruments; the S-shaped fence is an exaggerated diagram, and the fence was offset, not visibly bent beforehand.
proposed: In the 1906 earthquake, a fence crossing the San Andreas Fault was offset about 8.5 feet (about 2.6 m). (Card 16.c1 headline: "In 1906, a California fence that crossed the San Andreas was suddenly offset by about 2.6 m." Body: "The two halves ended up about 2.6 m apart. How the ground stored up that jump explains how this fault makes earthquakes.")

evidence: USGS Parkfield: locked sections produced the M 7.9 Fort Tejon earthquake of 1857 and the M 7.9 San Francisco earthquake of 1906; from San Juan Bautista to Parkfield the creeping section produces numerous small (mostly M=5 and smaller) earthquakes but no large ones.

USGS: from the 1906 ground displacement Reid concluded the quake involved an elastic rebound of stored elastic stress; the S-shaped fence diagram greatly exaggerates the distortion, which is spread over many miles and can only be seen with precise instrumentation (e.g. GPS).
problem: The fact and card 16.c3 say the stored strain bends fences into an S shape, drawing "a straight fence into an S shape"; learners will take that literally. USGS says that S shape is a greatly exaggerated diagram: the real bending is spread over many miles and invisible to the eye.
proposed: Studying how the ground moved in 1906, Henry Fielding Reid concluded that earthquakes are an 'elastic rebound': as the plates move, the crust beside a locked fault slowly bends and stores elastic strain, spread over many miles and too gentle to see without precise instruments, then releases it suddenly. (Card 16.c3: replace "drawing a straight fence into an S shape" with "so gently, over many miles, that only precise instruments can see it; diagrams draw it as a fence bent into an S shape".)

evidence: USGS This Dynamic Earth: the San Andreas fault zone is about 1,300 km long, slicing through California; land on the Pacific Plate moves northwesterly relative to the North American Plate.
USGS: the shaking from the M6.7 Northridge earthquake was more intense and covered a wider area than the slightly larger M6.8 Nisqually earthquake; Northridge 3-11 miles deep, Nisqually 30-36 miles.
USGS: "Bedrock shakes the least, and soft mud the most" (three stations equidistant from the 1989 Loma Prieta quake).
USGS: liquefaction is when water-saturated sediment temporarily loses strength and acts like a fluid, like wiggling your toes in wet sand at the beach; sand boils pictured.

Britannica: moment magnitude 6.9; epicenter near Loma Prieta peak about 60 miles south of San Francisco; the Marina was particularly hard hit because it had been built on filled land of loose, sandy soil.
USGS: an earthquake has a single magnitude; shaking varies from place to place based on distance and ground; intensities in Roman numerals on the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale in the US.
USGS FAQ: in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, liquefaction of lagoon fill caused major subsidence, fracturing and horizontal sliding of the ground surface in the Marina district.
USGS Volcanoes (types): in 1943 a cinder cone started growing on a farm near the village of Paricutin in Mexico; during 9 years of activity it built a prominent cone.
NPS: gases can escape more easily from thin fluids than thick ones, as can be observed in the spattering that can happen when making jam.
USGS: shield volcanoes are built by the accretion of thousands of highly fluid basalt lava flows into a broad, gently sloping cone; Mauna Loa is the world's largest active volcano.

NPS: viscosity is resistance to flow; higher silica gives longer, more complex chains that tangle like long strands of spaghetti; high-silica magmas are highly viscous and gas-trapping, low-silica ones runny.
USGS: composite volcanoes (stratovolcanoes) are steep, symmetrical cones built of alternating layers of lava flows, ash, cinders, blocks and bombs; examples include Mount Fuji and Mount St. Helens.
USGS Fact Sheet 027-00: small jagged pieces of rocks, minerals and volcanic glass less than 2 millimeters; not like the soft material of burning wood; hard; wind can carry ash thousands of miles.
USGS VHP: by far the most abundant volcanic gas is water vapor, which is harmless; significant amounts of carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are also emitted.

USGS VHP: deaths caused directly by lava flows are uncommon because most move slowly enough that people can move out of the way; everything in the path is knocked over, buried or ignited; homes and land can be buried under tens of meters of rock.
Britannica: the eruption of May 8, 1902, a nuee ardente (fiery cloud), destroyed Saint-Pierre. NatGeo notes the pyroclastic flow swept into St. Pierre, Martinique.
National Geographic: pyroclastic flows are considered the most deadly of all volcano hazards.

USGS VHP: a high-density mix of hot lava blocks, pumice, ash and volcanic gas; speeds typically greater than 80 km per hour; 200 to 700 degrees C; knock down, shatter, bury or carry away nearly all objects.

NPS: the Cascade volcanoes extend from southern British Columbia to northern California above the Cascadia subduction zone; magmas high in silica are thick and pasty, gases may be trapped, so Cascades volcanoes can be explosive.
USGS: the world's largest earthquakes (magnitude 9+) occur in subduction zones, where one tectonic plate is sliding under another.

LibreTexts Physical Geology: CO2 reacts with water to produce carbonic acid that dissolves calcite; biological processes in soil produce a much higher CO2 concentration, so water percolating through soil becomes significantly more acidic.
LibreTexts (Johnson et al.): carbonic acid reacts with minerals such as feldspars to form clay minerals; the Sierra College text adds that quartz is virtually unaffected by chemical weathering.
LibreTexts (Panchuk): the effectiveness of frost wedging depends on how often freezing and thawing occur; most effective where temperatures swing between warm and freezing.
USGS Water Science School: upon freezing, the density of ice decreases by about 9 percent (it expands about 9%). LibreTexts (Panchuk): water in cracks expands on freezing and enlarges them.
LibreTexts Physical Geology: when the olivine in basalt is oxidized, the basalt takes on a reddish color very different from the dark grey or black of unweathered basalt.
LibreTexts (Johnson et al.): root wedging happens when plant roots work themselves into cracks, prying the bedrock apart as they grow.

Britannica: weathering is disintegration or alteration of rock in its original position at or near the surface; physical (mechanical) and chemical weathering; erosion includes transportation away from the site.
NPS Solution Caves: caves form in limestone, dolomite, gypsum and halite and are associated with karst landscapes; the page describes sinking streams and sinkholes as parts of the cave system.
Britannica: mapped passages with a combined length of at least 400 miles (650 km), the longest cave system in the world; formed by dissolution of limestone by water.

USGS: sinkholes are common where the rock is limestone, carbonate rock, salt beds or other soluble rock (evaporites include salt and gypsum); cover-collapse sinkholes may develop abruptly (over a period of hours).
Britannica: the simplest stalactite is a thin-walled stone straw. NPS Speleothems: all stalactites begin their growth as hollow soda straws.
NPS: CO2 mixes with rainfall and snowmelt most often in the soil, making carbonic acid; the acidified water percolates down until it reaches the limestone, dissolving rock along joints and fractures.
Britannica: stalactites hang from the ceiling, stalagmites rise from the floor, mainly calcite, deposited as carbon dioxide escapes; when they meet they can form columns.

Earle, Physical Geology: on a curved section of a stream, flow is fastest on the outside and slowest on the inside. National Geographic (Oxbow lake): outer (concave) banks erode; silt and sediment build up on convex banks.
National Geographic: the river cuts off meanders, forming oxbow lakes; the name comes from the U-shaped collar placed around an ox's neck.
Earle: bed load moved by saltation (bouncing) and traction; smaller particles held in suspension; the dissolved load is on average about 15% of the mass transported, with ions such as calcium.
Earle: the Hjulstrom-Sundborg diagram relates particle size to the current velocities at which grains are eroded, transported or deposited; below a threshold velocity particles settle.
LibreTexts (Fullerton): stream-carved canyons have a V-shaped profile; glaciers are wider and erode both their bases and sides, turning V-shaped valleys into U shapes.
National Geographic, Delta: a river moves more slowly as it nears its mouth, so sediment falls to the bottom; a mature deltaic lobe includes a network of distributaries branching off the main river.
National Geographic: the term delta comes from the upper-case Greek letter delta, shaped like a triangle; the Nile forms an arcuate delta; the Mississippi forms a bird-foot delta.

National Geographic, Floodplain: a generally flat area next to a river; floods carry nutrient-rich silt, making floodplains very fertile; ancient Egyptian culture developed around the fertile floodplains of the Nile.
National Geographic, Overbank deposits: coarser, heavier sediment settles first and builds up the banks of the river, whereas finer sediment is carried farther away before it settles.
National Geographic: the Nile delta is shrinking as a result of the Aswan Dam and other river management; without sediment, Mediterranean waves erode it faster than the Nile can replace it.
NPS: cirques are bowl-shaped depressions glaciers carve high on mountains; lakes (tarns) often occupy them once the glaciers retreat. National Geographic: alpine glaciers begin to flow from cirques.
Britannica: a fjord is a long narrow arm of the sea resulting from marine inundation of a glaciated valley. NPS: fjord floors are below sea level and so are inundated with ocean water.
Britannica, Horn: three or more cirques erode into a mountain from multiple sides, leaving aretes that converge at a horn; the Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps is a famous example.
Britannica, Glacial erosion: plucking, ice freezing onto bedrock and pulling pieces away; abrasion, rocks embedded in the ice grind the bedrock, creating scratches (striations) and polish.
Britannica, Fjord: Sogn Fjord in Norway reaches 1,308 m (4,290 feet) deep.
NPS: valley glaciers concentrate erosion over the entire valley, widening its floor and over-steepening its walls, leaving a steep-walled, flat-bottomed U-shaped valley.

USGS Deserts (Eolian processes): deflation is the removal of loose, fine-grained particles by wind; most deflation zones are desert pavement, a sheetlike surface of rock fragments left after fines are removed.
USGS Desert Features: sand covers only about 20 percent of Earth's deserts; nearly 50 percent of desert surfaces are plains where deflation has exposed loose gravels.

NPS Aeolian Landforms: most dunes have a long shallow slope facing into the wind, a crest and a steep lee side; USGS Dunes names the steep side the slipface; NPS Sleeping Bear: active dunes gradually advance.
USGS: saltation moves sand-size particles downwind in a series of short hops, normally no more than one centimeter above the ground.
USGS: ventifacts are rocks cut, and sometimes polished, by the abrasive action of wind; yardangs are up to tens of meters high and kilometers long, streamlined by desert winds.

USGS FAQ: debris flows are fast-moving landslides that can travel at speeds up to and exceeding 35 mph; USGS post-fire page: mixtures of water, mud, rocks and vegetation that can surge downslope like flowing concrete.
problem: The fact is right, but card 27.c4 opens "Debris flows are the fastest kind", an unsourced superlative: rock falls and rock avalanches can move faster. USGS calls debris flows fast-moving and particularly dangerous, not the fastest.
proposed: Debris flows are fast-moving landslides of water, mud, rocks and vegetation that can surge downslope like flowing concrete, often faster than a person can run and at speeds that can exceed 35 mph. (Card 27.c4: change "Debris flows are the fastest kind:" to "Debris flows are among the fastest and most dangerous kinds:".)

evidence: USGS FAQ: a landslide is the movement of a mass of rock, debris or earth down a slope; it occurs when down-slope forces (mainly gravity) exceed the strength of the earth materials; five modes: falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows.

USGS FAQ: triggers include rainfall, snowmelt, changes in water level, stream erosion, changes in ground water, earthquakes, volcanic activity and human disturbance. USGS debris-flow FAQ: they occur in all 50 states and US territories.
USGS: after a fire vegetation is removed and soil properties change, reducing the ground's ability to absorb rainfall, so even modest rainstorms can trigger debris flows in steep burned areas.
Britannica, Landslide: oversteepening of the base of the slope, such as by natural erosion or excavation, builds up stresses.
Britannica: in sandy materials increased water reduces interparticle friction; a rise in the groundwater table adds load to the slope.
NPS Arches: there are over 2,000 documented arches in the park.

NPS Arches: a salt layer bulged upward into long domes and the covering rock cracked into more-or-less parallel lines; water dissolves the calcite bonding the sand and freezing water pries rock apart, turning fins into arches.
NPS Bryce Canyon: the (slightly) acidic rain is enough to dissolve the calcium carbonate that holds these rocks together.
NPS Bryce Canyon: the Bryce Amphitheater is home to the greatest concentration of hoodoos on Earth.
National Geographic, Butte: buttes are created as streams cut through a mesa or plateau; the hard caprock resists weathering and erosion and protects the more vulnerable rock beneath.
NPS Life of Hoodoos wayside: harder caprock preserves softer rocks below as fins; frost wedging forms holes called windows; as windows expand, the caprock collapses, leaving hoodoos.
NPS: mesas are broad flat-topped mountains with at least one steep side; buttes are smaller with steep slopes on all sides. National Geographic: a butte is usually taller than it is wide.

NPS: the Appalachians formed during a collision of continents 500 to 300 million years ago, probably had peaks as high as the modern Himalayas-to-Alps collision zone, and have eroded over the past 300 million years.
Britannica: Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, 29,032 feet (8,849 meters); the 2020 China-Nepal survey gave 8,848.86 m.
USGS This Dynamic Earth: the Himalayas began to form 40 to 50 million years ago when India and Eurasia collided and continue to rise more than 1 cm a year, a growth rate of 10 km in a million years.

Britannica: high mountains have low-density roots extending deep into the mantle, analogous to an iceberg. Earle (LibreTexts): when weight is removed by erosion over tens of millions of years, the crust rebounds.
Britannica, Appalachian Mountains: the system reaches its highest summit on Mount Mitchell, 6,684 feet (2,037 metres).
NPS Valley and Ridge: limestones and shales are more susceptible to erosion and make up much of the valleys, whereas more resistant sandstones and conglomerates form the ridges.
NPS Mississippi River facts: the river drains all or parts of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental United States.
NCSE quotes Playfair on Siccar Point: "The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time."

Britannica: Hutton (1726 to 1797) presented papers to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785; erosion, deposition, sedimentation and upthrusting were cyclical and repeated many times, so the age of the Earth must be inconceivably great.

Geological Society: at Siccar Point nearly vertical Silurian greywacke sandstones and mudstones are covered unconformably by younger red sandstone and breccia. NCSE defines an unconformity as a surface where rocks formed at different times meet.

NCSE: because sediments form horizontally, Hutton knew the vertical beds had been tilted and raised above land; erosion wore them away, then they were submerged and covered by new horizontal sediment.

NCSE: during June 1788 James Hutton, with John Playfair and James Hall, visited Siccar Point on the Berwickshire coast. Britannica and the Geological Society: Hutton had already presented his theory of an immensely old Earth in 1785; Siccar Point was evidence that helped him demonstrate it.
problem: The fact is right, but hook card 31.c1 says the cliff "convinced James Hutton" Earth was far older and that it "made Earth unimaginably old". Hutton had already argued this in 1785 (card 31.c2 says so); Siccar Point, in 1788, was the evidence that proved his case to others.
proposed: In June 1788 James Hutton, with John Playfair and James Hall, visited Siccar Point on the Berwickshire coast of Scotland. (Card 31.c1: headline "In 1788, a rocky Scottish point showed that Earth is unimaginably old."; body sentence "One cliff on the Scottish coast convinced James Hutton it had to be far, far older." becomes "One cliff on the Scottish coast gave James Hutton striking proof that it was far, far older.")

evidence: Britannica: contemporary geology accepted that Earth was created only about 6,000 years ago, following Genesis; Hutton's theory contradicted this.
NPS: younger rocks or structures cut across older rocks or structures; an intrusive rock body is younger than the rocks it intrudes; faults are younger than the rock layers they cut.
NPS, Cross-cutting relationships: erosional surfaces are younger than the rocks they erode.

UCMP Berkeley: Steno's ideas were published in 1669; original horizontality, rock layers form horizontally; superposition, oldest on the bottom and youngest on top unless later processes disturb the arrangement.
Understanding Evolution (Berkeley): superposition sometimes does not work because layers were overturned or older rock pushed up over younger rock, as can happen when great mountain belts form.
UCMP Berkeley: Steno's law is a statement of relative time, not absolute time: two layers could have formed millions of years apart or a few hours or days apart.
Britannica, Index fossil: commonly used marine index fossils include single-celled protists and larger forms such as ammonoids.
USGS Geologic Time: because fossils record the slow but progressive development of life, scientists use them to identify rocks of the same age throughout the world.
Britannica: a useful index fossil must be distinctive or easily recognizable, abundant, and have a wide geographic distribution and a short range through time.
UCMP Berkeley: Smith was the first to use fossils to map rocks by stratigraphic order; with 400 subscribers, production began in 1812 and in 1815 the map was published (of England and Wales).

UCMP Berkeley: William Smith (1769-1839), a surveyor supervising the Somerset Canal from the 1790s, observed fossils always in a certain order from bottom to top, and the same order elsewhere: the principle of faunal succession.
USGS Geologic Time: carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years and finds its way into all living plants and animals; the clock can be used only within the past 50,000 years.

USGS: radiometric dating measures the last time the rock was melted or disturbed enough to rehomogenize its radioactive elements. Understanding Evolution (Berkeley): most fossils cannot be dated directly; volcanic ash or other igneous rocks can.

USGS: in radioactive decay a parent isotope forms an isotope of a new element (the daughter); half-life is the time for one-half of a radioactive isotope in a sample to decay; slow decayers serve as geologic clocks.
USGS table: uranium-238 to lead-206, currently accepted half-life 4.5 billion years, used to date ancient rocks.
OPB/NPR: zircon loves uranium and will take it in as it grows, but zircon hates lead, so lead inside it pretty surely came from uranium decay.

USGS: comparing lead isotopes in Earth's oldest lead ores with the primordial composition in uranium-free phases of iron meteorites (Canyon Diablo) gives 4.54 billion years with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent.
UW-Madison News (2014): zircons, the oldest known terrestrial materials, from Western Australia's Jack Hills crystallized 4.4 billion years ago. USGS: found in younger sedimentary rocks.

USGS: Earth and the Solar System's other bodies formed at the same time; meteorites, fragments of asteroids, give the best ages; more than 70 meteorites formed between 4.53 and 4.58 billion years ago.
USGS: scientists have not found a way to determine Earth's exact age directly from Earth rocks because the oldest rocks have been recycled and destroyed by plate tectonics.
Geology.com: zircon is highly resistant to chemical alteration and abrasion and can survive several cycles of uplift, weathering, erosion and deposition, persisting for billions of years.
Britannica, Geologic time: fossil forms in the rocks provide the chief means of establishing a geologic time scale; the appearance and disappearance of species mark interval boundaries.
ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart v2024/12 lists the eons Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic; the USGS 2018 time scale fact sheet shows the same four.
ICS chart v2024/12: Holocene Epoch of the Quaternary Period, Cenozoic Era, Phanerozoic Eon is the current unit.
Smithsonian Human Origins: during a time of dramatic climate change 300,000 years ago, Homo sapiens evolved in Africa.

ICS chart v2024/12 puts the base of the Phanerozoic (Cambrian, Paleozoic) at 538.8 plus or minus 0.6 million years ago; Mesozoic from 251.902 and Cenozoic from 66.0 Ma. Britannica still gives the older 541 figure and says the eon is about the last one-eighth of time since the crust formed.
problem: The Paleozoic start date of 541 million years ago is the pre-2022 value; the tree rules require the International Commission on Stratigraphy chart, which now gives 538.8 million years ago. (The one-eighth and the 252 and 66 figures are fine; no card shows 541.)
proposed: The Phanerozoic, the eon of visible life, covers only about the last one-eighth of the time since Earth's crust formed; its three eras are the Paleozoic (about 539 to 252 million years ago), the Mesozoic (252 to 66 million years ago) and the Cenozoic (66 million years ago to today).

evidence: Britannica: eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages in descending order; the International Chronostratigraphic Chart is maintained by the International Commission on Stratigraphy.

Natural History Museum: oxygen from ocean bacteria combined with dissolved iron to form insoluble iron oxide that sank, laying red iron-oxide sheets between silica-rich layers; once soluble iron was bound up, free oxygen went into the atmosphere.
Britannica: iron oxides (hematite with secondary magnetite and others) alternating with chert or quartz; usually older than 1.7 billion years; used as low-grade iron ore.
Britannica, Evolution of the atmosphere: blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), through photosynthesis, converted carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates, releasing free oxygen.
NASA Astrobiology: oxygen did not make up a significant portion of the atmosphere until after the Great Oxidation Event, roughly 2.45 billion years ago.
Britannica: the Great Oxidation Event began roughly 2.4 billion years ago. NASA Astrobiology gives roughly 2.45 billion years ago.
Britannica: layered deposit, mainly limestone, formed by blue-green algae; the earliest date back about 3.5 billion years; modern ones thrive in Shark Bay, Western Australia.
